items.summary: Chris Emanuel, managing director and head of GIC's Technology Investment Group, said on a LinkedIn post dated Nov 20 that the Singapore sovereign wealth fund intends to remain invested in Anthropic beyond its Nasdaq debut. He described this as 'life-cycle investing,' noting GIC participated in three funding rounds in under a year and is now one of Anthropic's largest investors. The article attributes several figures to specific sources: Bloomberg reported GIC has invested more than US$4.5 billion across the last three rounds, with its stake valued at about US$15 billion at the IPO price; the Financial Times estimated Spark Capital holds roughly US$11 billion and Lightspeed Venture Partners a stake worth more than US$25 billion based on valuations attributed to Reuters; and The Business Times reported Anthropic's valuation climbed from US$61.5 billion in March 2025 to US$965 billion in its May 2026 private-funding round, with annualised revenue reaching about US$81 billion last month per Reuters. These are estimates or forecasts rather than audited results. GIC's involvement extended beyond capital through infrastructure support via Theseus and an investment in Ode that helps enterprises deploy Anthropic's technology.
items.title: GIC says it will stay invested in Anthropic after its record IPO

items.summary: Pessimism over the AI trade drove Asian equities lower and global markets toward their longest losing streak since September 2023. MSCI's Asia Pacific index fell 1.7% on Nov 20 to extend its decline to a seventh straight session, while the MSCI All Country World Index was poised for its longest slide since that same period. Anthropic, maker of Claude, declined over 5% in after-hours trading to below US$92 (S$118.80), slipping beneath its lowest debut level from Nov 19 despite having closed 17% above IPO price; the drop followed reports that Apple is developing its own AI agent. Charu Chanana of Saxo Markets said investors are questioning whether frontier AI remains a profitable business, and Matt Maley of Miller Tabak noted the Anthropic IPO does not address broader concerns about AI profitability, spending, higher interest rates, credit stress, and geopolitical risk. Elsewhere, emerging-market currencies weakened as dollar strength hovered near its highest since April 2025, the Bloomberg Commodity Index fell to its lowest since July, Treasuries rallied on haven demand, S&P 500 futures dropped 0.3%, and Nasdaq 100 contracts fell 0.6% after closing at their lowest level since April. Oil swung amid Middle East re-escalation concerns: WTI traded near US$83 a barrel (down 5% for the week) and Brent settled near US$92. Gold headed for its biggest weekly decline since March as hawkish Fed comments pushed rate-hike expectations, falling to near US$3,590 an ounce on Nov 20 after losing more than 7% in a week that saw it slide to September 2025 lows; silver lost around 13% over the same period. The 10-year Treasury yield at around 5.02% was poised to match its 2007 run of 29 closes above 5%, and traders expect a December Fed hike followed by two more increases in 2027; Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee said he would consider all options, including larger-than-usual hikes, citing persistently high inflation. No visual is warranted: the reported figures measure different assets (equity indices, an IPO price, oil, gold/silver, and Treasury yields) rather than comparable quantities across a single set of names.
items.title: Asian stocks fall, Anthropic slips in after-hours: Markets wrap

items.summary: Anthropic closed its initial public offering roughly 17% above its offer price at just over $97 a share, valuing the company near $1.7tn after briefly exceeding $2tn during trading; with demand about six times supply, it raised $81bn from 980m shares to become the largest IPO in history, surpassing SpaceX's prior record of $75bn. Despite this milestone, major US indexes fell to seven-month lows amid concerns over AI's longer-term outlook, and Asian stocks plunged up to 4% on Friday as Anthropic appeared unable to settle market nerves. The company reported $16.2bn in revenue for the first half of 2026 versus $4.6bn across all of 2025, but posted losses that grew from a one-off-charge-driven $80bn figure to $104bn over nine months, with costs expected to rise further as it plans roughly $900bn in datacentre spending over two decades. Anthropic faces additional headwinds: growing public opposition to AI has produced local bans on datacentres at recent midterms, and Senator Elizabeth Warren signaled that the IPO could inject volatility into the financial system, though she argued its cash-burning model should not expose everyday investors to such risk. Analyst Bob O'Donnell of TECHnalysis Research said real stability depends on OpenAI's outcome, Nvidia developments, datacentre policy, and Anthropic's historical performance; meanwhile OpenAI postponed its own offering until 2027 but CEO Sam Altman indicated it would proceed next year, citing excessive demand relative to supply. Jason Furman of Harvard estimated that investment in information processing equipment and software accounted for 92% of US GDP growth in the first half of 2025, underscoring how a slowdown could affect both Anthropic and the broader economy.
items.title: Anthropic's record-breaking IPO debut, its financials, and looming regulatory uncertainty

items.summary: AINews reports Anthropic set its Nasdaq IPO price at $83 and that the ticker ANT closed at $97.17, up 17% from the offering price (drifting -5% to $92.60 after close). The AINews item states the $81.3B raise overtook SpaceX's June IPO as the largest in history; this is attributed to AINews and not independently verified here. Co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei issued remarks pledging to pace training and deployment until systems remain safe and under human control, a claim sourced directly from their statements. The item notes Class F shares carry 50.1% of voting power on most matters (attributed), that about a trillion dollars of shares are expected to free up over the next year as lockups expire (attributed), and that AMD agreed to invest $2.5B alongside the IPO (attributed). The AINews item frames several financial figures—low cash burn, bear-case revenue math requiring ~$602B/yr, median employee take-home near ~$5M after taxes—as analyst or investor claims rather than established facts; these are attributed to their respective sources. No tables of figures appear in the item, so no visual is warranted.
items.title: Anthropic IPO priced at $83, closed up 17% to $97.17 on a record $81.3B raise

items.summary: PostgreSQL 19 reached general availability and Lakebase made it available to customers the same day, contrasting with other managed services that typically take weeks. The Lakebase team includes several PostgreSQL committers who contributed directly to this release. Version 19 is characterized by operational improvements rather than a single headline feature: REPACK reclaims space like VACUUM FULL and physically orders rows via USING INDEX while continuing normal reads and writes during most of the operation, though it requires free capacity under max_repack_replication_slots, an index-based replica identity or non-deferrable primary key, temporary disk for table copies plus sort files, and fails if more than about 104 million tuples are updated or deleted on a busy table while REPACK CONCURRENTLY runs. pg_plan_advice and pg_stash_advice let teams intervene when inaccurate statistics produce poor plans without adding cross-table statistics or replacing the planner; matched feedback indicates plan compliance but not necessarily improvement. Additional changes include parallel autovacuum index workers with autovacuum_max_parallel_workers, new statistics views (pg_stat_lock, pg_stat_recovery, pg_stat_autovacuum_scores), EXPLAIN IO and WAL reporting, logical replication improvements including wal_level replica behavior, sequence synchronization on subscription creation, WAIT FOR LSN for read-replica handoff coordination, remote statistics import in postgres_fdw, INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO SELECT returning existing and new rows, JSON output from COPY TO (export-only by default), and function support for date types. Several features were removed before release due to correctness or design concerns: SQL/PGQ property graph queries reverted September 7, UPDATE and DELETE FOR PORTION OF on September 15, ALTER TABLE MERGE/SPLIT PARTITIONS on August 27, GROUP BY ALL on July 17, pg_dumpall on June 18, and several DDL functions on September 13. Lakebase notes that PostgreSQL 19.1 is anticipated in February as the typical first minor release after a major version.
items.title: Lakebase offers PostgreSQL 19 GA on its managed service same day as release

items.summary: In a forum post, Julia Yeo reports paying $15.23 for a bottle of mometasone nasal spray with 140 doses in May 2026 at a private hospital, then being charged $64 for two bottles of the same medication in November, or $32 per bottle. She acknowledges that commercial factors such as procurement costs and suppliers can drive price changes but argues patients managing chronic conditions should not have to compare pharmacy prices after every consultation. Yeo proposes that private hospitals explain substantial medication price increases and inform patients when more affordable equivalent alternatives exist, framing transparency as a balance against the hospital's commercial interests.
items.title: A patient's letter proposing that private hospitals disclose medication price increases and cheaper alternatives

items.summary: In a forum post titled 'Repeated construction of condo showflats affects residents,' resident Chiang Chee Keong raises concerns about vacant land on Prince Charles Crescent that faces his residential unit and has been repeatedly used for condominium showflats. He states the structures are temporary, demolished and rebuilt periodically for different developments, so he experiences recurring construction noise rather than a one-off disturbance. Regarding the latest showflat, he reports an ongoing humming from generators audible from his residence even after completion, which he says feedback to the developer has not resolved. He acknowledges developers need facilities to market projects but asks authorities to review how such sites near residential developments are managed, including noise mitigation, repeated demolition and rebuilding, and prolonged reliance on generators.
items.title: Resident complains to authorities over repeated condo showflat construction noise

items.summary: Henrijs Dandzbergs, a 16-year-old born in Latvia who is too young to vote or drink, was admitted as likely the youngest solo founder in Y Combinator's history when he joined its fall 2026 cohort. His startup, Polemos Industries, aims to develop precision-guided missiles that are cheaply and easily manufactured, fired from portable launchers, resistant to jamming, more precise than widely deployed drones, capable of carrying larger warheads, and cheaper than large rocket systems—guided by the ambition to lower the 'cost per kill.' Dandzbergs originally competed in a Unicorn Mafia hackathon with two older teammates, Aleksandrs Tihenko and Kai Yang, building an AI system that designs circuit boards from natural-language prompts; they won but later parted ways over whether to focus on defense. Y Combinator initially tried to steer him away given his age and the seriousness of the venture, but admitted him once it judged there was a non-zero chance the idea could work. Competitors include Anduril, CoAspire, and Leidos. Polemos has reportedly developed its missile-guidance software and begun hardware design, with Dandzbergs hoping to showcase a prototype when the program ends in December—though this is stated as his hope rather than an accomplished result. Tom Karako of CSIS notes trade-offs: cheap missiles may sacrifice range, payload, or reliability. The startup publicly announced itself on November 5 via a social-media video showing four missiles destroying a convoy; Dandzbergs responded to comparisons with Palmer Luckey, Anduril's cofounder who started his first company at 19. Dandzbergs frames autonomous weapons as inevitable and claims pure protective motivations, while McKenzie-Wilson, the Unicorn Mafia director who left his own drone startup after it added payloads, says he could not know in advance how someone would handle building a weapon that kills people—predicting Dandzbergs may later confront this himself.
items.title: 16-year-old Henrijs Dandzbergs admitted to Y Combinator's fall 2026 cohort for AI-guided-missile startup Polemos Industries

items.summary: In an interview, Peter Gabriel discusses his 13-track, nearly 90-minute album o:i, its two versions produced by Tchad Blake and Mike 'Spike' Stent, and his promotion of AI as a creative tool. He asserts that AI will ultimately do things better than humans in music, though he adds caveats about the dangers of AI and robots in warfare and calls for international agreements with guard rails on algorithm release; these views are attributed to him rather than established fact. He also describes collaborations involving bonobo Kanzi communicating musically via sign language and a speech-synthesis keyboard developed by primatologist Sue Savage-Rumbaugh, Michael Levin's work on morphogenesis including growing an eye on a frog leg, experiments suggesting plant sentience at MIT, and plans for brain-computer interfaces he calls becoming cyborgs. His track record of anticipating industry shifts is cited as supporting his forward-looking views: being the first British artist to own a sampler in the early 1980s, co-founding a streaming platform that competed with Spotify, and leaving Genesis when progressive rock became too grandiloquent; these are presented as past events. The interview notes o:i continues the project begun with i/o (2023), his first new material in 21 years, including songs like A Hard Lesson started in 1989 while he was a mainstream pop star after So shifted more than 5m copies in the US alone; these figures are reported as stated. Gabriel attributes his lengthy album-making process to being easily distracted and valuing diverse interests over finishing quickly.
items.title: Peter Gabriel interview covering his new album o:i and his advocacy for AI in music

items.summary: Analytics platform Sensor Tower estimates GTA 6's pre-orders and first-day sales reached more than 24.5 million units, worth about $2.36bn (£1.8bn), making it the largest entertainment launch in history; this figure is an estimate from email receipts data rather than a confirmed total, since Rockstar and parent company Take-Two have not released official sales details but described demand as "unprecedented." For context, Sensor Tower notes that this first-day gross exceeds Spider-Man: Brand New Day's $2.5bn cinema run only over the game's single day versus the film's entire release window, so the comparison is of different scopes rather than a direct tie. The PlayStation 5 accounted for around three quarters of sales with Xbox covering the balance. Niko Partners separately forecasts more than $3bn in worldwide sales this year and estimates that GTA 6 will still fall short of 1939's Gone with the Wind, which has made an estimated $4.5bn adjusted for inflation; both are projections rather than measured results. The game is estimated to have cost over $1bn to develop, making it potentially the most expensive video game in history, though this remains an estimate and a claim of record status. Sensor Tower also projects that GTA 6's popularity will reduce time spent on other single-player titles by 10%, which is another forecast rather than observed data.
items.title: GTA 6 estimated to be biggest entertainment launch after first-day sales top $2.3bn

items.summary: A University of Liège team modeled one representative semi-detached dwelling, selected from 708 audited homes and calibrated against four years of measured gas and electricity use. Adding a 5 kWh battery to an existing heat pump and rooftop PV reduced annual grid imports from 40.0 kWh/m² (solar alone) to 33.2 kWh/m², a drop of 6.8 kWh/m² or 17%, while net annual energy use stayed identical across the three solar-plus-storage configurations. Operational emissions fell by another 14% versus solar alone. Battery capacity gains show diminishing returns: the first 2 kWh saved 0.43 kg CO₂e per square meter per year, and expanding to 5 kWh added only 0.31 over that range; at 5 kWh the home already used 95% of its own generation, leaving little surplus for a larger battery under this control strategy. The researchers tested two sizes rather than pin down a precise threshold. Replacing the gas boiler with a heat pump gave the largest single carbon cut (67%), and adding PV plus the 5 kWh battery brought total operational emissions from 18.46 to 4.64 kg CO₂e per square meter per year, or 75% overall. Grid imports remained concentrated in winter evenings when solar output was insufficient. The study did not quantify electricity bill savings or investment payback; the reported figures are model-based estimates for one building and depend on heating demand, fuel replaced, heat pump efficiency, solar output, and local hourly emissions, so results do not generalize beyond this case.
items.title: Heat pump plus solar-plus-storage retrofit cuts grid electricity imports by 17% in a Belgian home model

items.summary: A severe storm cell on Thursday 19 November 2026 destroyed two transmission towers on the 132 kV line between Cultana and Port Lincoln, according to a state of emergency declaration. Transmission operator ElectraNet reported about 24,000 customers lost power regionwide; by Friday's update roughly 10,000 properties remained without supply while crews worked temporary solutions that could take several days. Energy Minister Tom Koutsantonis declared an electricity supply emergency under the Energy Management Act 2004 for a period of 14 days unless revoked earlier, authorizing use of a diesel generator in Port Lincoln and directing AEMO to seek spare generation. Because Port Lincoln had become islanded from the National Electricity Market, SAPN asked households there with rooftop solar panels to switch them off until advised otherwise so they would not trip the temporary generators; Koutsantonis said this advice did not apply outside that region. The incident prompted comparisons to the 2016 statewide blackout caused by a cascading failure after storm damage in the Mid North, though MP Sam Tefler noted this event was more localized and raised questions about energy security once restoration completes.
items.title: South Australia declares electricity supply emergency after storm damages transmission infrastructure

items.summary: Brent crude traded at $92.67 per barrel and WTI at $83.06 per barrel, reversing an earlier-week decline after reports that Yemen's Houthis struck targets in Riyadh including the financial district and sovereign wealth fund headquarters plus a Jubail petrochemicals company, alongside IRGC claims of daily tanker mine strikes in the Strait of Hormuz this month with two reported explosions on Thursday. These developments counter supply-glut narratives: the International Energy Agency predicted an oil surplus returning this quarter extending into next year, while investment banks claimed oversupply as Persian Gulf exports rebounded to pre-war levels and exceeded them. Oil and gas flow trackers dispute that view, noting exports have improved since early in the war but remain below pre-war levels and may have declined after a September peak amid tightened strait transit enforcement in October and November.
items.title: Crude prices rebound on Houthi attacks and Strait of Hormuz tanker incidents

items.summary: ACME Solar Holdings Limited reports that its wholly owned subsidiary ACME Sigma Urja Private Limited commissioned a Firm and Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE) facility of 57.69 MW on November 19, 2026, in Kharnai village under Rawatbhata tehsil in Chittorgarh district, Rajasthan. The site combines 100.02 MW of installed solar capacity with a Battery Energy Storage System rated at 57.69 MW / 265.38 MWh and is connected to the Neemuch Pooling Station for power evacuation. ACME Solar states that BESS integration will store electricity generated by solar arrays so it can be dispatched when required, thereby improving supply flexibility and grid reliability; this characterization of benefit is a company claim rather than an independently verified outcome. The commercial operation date (COD) was scheduled for November 21, 2026, and the company reports securing a Power Purchase Agreement with NHPC Limited to sell renewable electricity from the project. This commissioned phase represents one stage toward completing ACME Solar's larger 250 MW FDRE project; the text frames it as an important step but does not establish that completion is assured or on schedule.
items.title: ACME Solar commissions 57.69 MW FDRE capacity in Rajasthan with BESS, COD set for November 21, 2026.

items.summary: The source frames Nvidia as a dominant force in AI, with influence extending beyond GPUs into an integrated ecosystem of software, networking and data-centre solutions. It asserts that Jensen Huang has departed as CEO and poses the question of whether Nvidia can maintain its innovation advantage amid this leadership change. The text presents this transition as consequential for the broader semiconductor industry, global AI competition and software integration, but offers no evidence or analysis to support these claims; it functions only as an unverified framing rather than a substantiated assessment.
items.title: Nvidia's leadership transition raises questions about sustaining its innovation edge after Jensen Huang

items.summary: Overseas brokerage Jefferies maintained positive ratings on selected Adani Group companies, including Adani Ports and SEZ Ltd (ADSEZ), Adani Power, Adani Green Energy, and Adani Energy Solutions, following their second-quarter results. The firm sees up to 35% upside potential in these stocks, which were trading higher at the time of reporting. Regarding ADSEZ specifically, Jefferies noted that management remains confident in achieving its one billion tonnes cargo target by 2030 (a 16% CAGR), with domestic port growth expected to remain organic and profitability-focused; international M&A is targeted toward margin-accretive assets in stable geographies offering long-term earnings visibility. These are Jefferies' published views, not established outcomes.
items.title: Jefferies rates select Adani Group stocks Buy with up to 35% upside after Q2 earnings

items.summary: The Trump administration issued new rules restricting remote computing access through data centres in third countries, closing a loophole that let Chinese companies bypass existing export controls on advanced Nvidia chips. The measures follow Jensen Huang's resignation after reports of an extramarital affair with Alice Huang, whom the New York Times reported US officials suspected was a Chinese spy; Beijing rejects these claims and calls the rules economic coercion. Alibaba warned its global data centre expansion plans could be affected while still assessing repercussions, despite reporting 53 per cent year-on-year growth in AI cloud revenue to nearly 61 billion yuan (US$9 billion) for July-September, with capital expenditures jumping 60 per cent to 50.5 billion yuan amid its Qwen4-Max launch and Zhenwu V900 chip promotion. Tencent's President Martin Lau said the rule "sets everyone back in China," noting reduced compute access would impact training timelines for its next AI models, while researcher James Chai of ISEAS noted Chinese firms remain heavily dependent on frontier Nvidia chips. A study by the Institute for Progress estimated remote overseas data centre access could account for roughly one-third of China's AI compute by end-2027; this is a forecast rather than an established figure and cannot be treated as fact. Nvidia said it was no longer shipping H200 chips, though some sales were greenlit after Huang's ouster. Analysts expect the US to intensify export controls further but also warn that tighter restrictions could accelerate China's push toward domestic chip self-sufficiency.
items.title: Chinese tech firms brace for AI disruption from new US chip restrictions

items.summary: A photo gallery presents several properties available for purchase across England, each marketed on its ability to admit natural daylight. The selection spans a grand house styled as a miniature fantasy castle and a converted Methodist chapel, among others shown in pictures.
items.title: Gallery of light-filled homes for sale in England

items.summary: Phillip Steer of March, Cambridgeshire, reports a 35% rise in players since 2022 following the pandemic, now around 100 across 15 venues in Fenland. Tom Brady of Live Pub Poker League also cites increased participation over the past 12 months. The £5 maximum stake and exempt-gaming status (no licence required; combined stakes capped at £100 daily) are offered as reasons for affordability, though Steer's causal link to the cost-of-living crisis is an opinion rather than a measured finding. Player accounts—Donald Rofe, Violet Cunningham—are anecdotal. The Gambling Commission states the rules but does not attribute growth.
items.title: Social poker with £5 stakes is growing in UK pubs, attributed to cost-of-living pressures

items.summary: A survey by Island Global Research found that more than 69% of respondents in Jersey, 68% in Guernsey and 70% in the Isle of Man noticed a rise in living costs over the past year. The study polled over 1,000 people on each island; 57% described themselves as less than comfortable financially, with about one in ten going without essentials such as food and heating. In Jersey, 10% reported they could not afford higher prices and often skipped basics, compared with 11% in Guernsey. Sixty-five percent said they now spend less on non-essentials while 53% shop around more due to price rises. Two-thirds of Jersey respondents found it hard to meet living costs over the last year, up 17 percentage points from 2024, and 58% in Guernsey reported similar difficulty. About one in four people received support for everyday expenses within six months; on the Isle of Man, 36% cut back on groceries and 30% received such financial help over that period.
items.title: Island survey finds major cost-of-living increase across Jersey, Guernsey and Isle of Man

items.summary: Dr Yanagizawa-Drott and Olaf Willner used an AI verifier on 1,000 APE (artificial production of economic) papers and found none error-free: 842 contained at least one severe error, some invalidating headline results. The Economist partnered with Refine to review 100 randomly chosen papers from the top five journals published in the first nine months of 2026 using several frontier AI models plus a human check; this flagged 4,158 issues and found at least one grave error in about one in ten papers. The two exercises are not directly comparable, but the lower rate among human economists suggests people retain an edge. Alexis Akira Toda of Emory University found that for economic-theory papers AI lowers the cost of checking a candidate flaw but does not yet reliably substitute for the human judgment that locates the flaw initially; another study comparing APE and published papers attributed most differences to ideas rather than execution. Michele Zampa of the Geneva Graduate Institute, grading 981 AI papers against 41 human ones on research-question novelty and acknowledgment of methodological limitations, found AI outperformed in crowded fields while humans performed at a constant level regardless of literature size. Benjamin Kohler of ETH Zürich and colleagues had AI reproduce 48 social-science papers from raw data and a methods description; discrepancies between originals and reproductions were roughly equal for AI and human work, but the balance tilted against humans as model quality improved.
items.title: AI verification finds errors in economics papers; human economists still show an edge

items.summary: Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Friday that Japan Tobacco's decision to cut its dividend would not hinder the government's industrial investment programme. The government owns a 37.55 per cent stake in Japan Tobacco and draws on dividend income from the company for such funding. Katayama told a news conference, "Even after the revision to the dividend forecast, there is no possibility that industrial investment will be hindered." Japan Tobacco lowered its annual dividend forecast by 25 per cent and expects a loss after losing control of Russian subsidiaries when President Vladimir Putin ordered their seizure in October; those units had accounted for around 25 per cent of group profits. Shares slumped more than 8 per cent early on Friday. The government booked 156 billion yen ($977.02 million) from its JT holdings into a special account for the year ended in March, at an exchange rate of $1 = 159.6700 yen.
items.title: Japan's finance minister says JT dividend cut will not disrupt industrial investment plans

items.summary: On Friday (Nov 20), TikTok announced a global launch of its "likeness detection tool," which lets politicians and accounts with large follower counts find and report AI-generated content using their image without consent. The rollout is gradual, and the company frames it as part of protecting European elections next year in Italy, France and Greece ahead of EU transparency rules requiring deepfake labelling from August. TikTok's government relations lead for European elections, Francesca Scapolo, said at a safety event in London that the tool would help politicians identify potentially AI-generated content shared without consent; AFP is among more than a dozen fact-checking organisations paid by TikTok to verify videos with potential false information.
items.title: TikTok launches global likeness detection tool for public figures

items.summary: Anthropic, maker of the Claude chatbot, raised $81.3 billion (€74bn) in its largest initial public offering on record, pricing shares at $83 to value the company at about $1.5 trillion (€1.36tn). The stock opened at $111.50 and closed Friday at $97.17, up 17.1% from the offer price after peaking near $115.10. Despite this strong debut, Asian shares fell sharply as an AI and chip sell-off spread from Wall Street; global stocks were on course for their longest losing streak in more than three years even after Nvidia beat earnings expectations. On Thursday the S&P 500 closed 2% lower, its sixth straight decline, while the Dow dropped 2.2% and the Nasdaq fell 2.3%. South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 both fell 4.5%, Australia's ASX 200 dropped 1.6%, Hong Kong's Hang Seng nearly 2%, and China's Shanghai Composite lost 1.7%. Gold and silver also fell as investors braced for a US rate rise: spot gold was down more than 4.5% to about $3,520 a troy ounce on course for its worst week in eight months, while spot silver fell 7% to $41.24 a troy ounce amid a dollar near a 19-month high. The sell-off reflected concerns that AI stocks had risen too far; Nvidia swung from a gain of 4.7% to a loss of 3.3%, and its co-founder Jensen Huang resigned as CEO last week. Japan's core inflation accelerated to 2.2% year on year in October, strengthening the case for a December rate rise, while China held benchmark lending rates unchanged at 3% one-year and 3.5% five-year. The report frames these moves as reactions to anticipated US interest-rate increases rather than established outcomes; Anthropic's share close of $97.17 is reported as an actual figure, whereas the gold and silver levels are described as positions on course for their worst weeks in eight months.
items.title: Anthropic's record IPO did not stop a global stock and precious-metals sell-off

items.summary: A train of 203 domestically made new energy vehicles departed Zhengzhou International Land Port on Thursday to mark the milestone of 10,000 special trains carrying exported finished vehicles. The shipment travels by rail to Shanghai's Minhang Station before transfer onto ro-ro ships for a roughly 14-day voyage to Australia covering more than 10,000 kilometers. Wang Xiaolu of China Railway Special Cargo Services Co., Ltd. said dedicated export vehicle trains entered regular service in 2021; the first 5,000 trains took about four years while reaching 10,000 took just over a year, which the company attributes to accelerating export volumes. Zhao Ruijie of Henan International Logistics Hub Construction and Operation Co., Ltd. said around three to four special vehicle trains run regularly from its hub daily, shipping 700 to 1,000 export vehicles per day. Since the start of this year more than 2.035 million finished vehicles have been exported via rail, a 79% year-on-year increase, according to these companies.
items.title: China's exported finished-vehicle rail shipments reach 10,000 dedicated trains

items.summary: Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said on Thursday that the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting marked a new peak in Asia-Pacific economic cooperation, describing it as China's most important diplomatic event of the year. The meeting produced the APEC Leaders' Shenzhen Outlook, which Wang called the most significant outcome of APEC's "China Year" and a new milestone in regional cooperation. Chinese President Xi Jinping proposed building an Asia-Pacific community characterized by solidarity, openness, innovation, and inclusive development, while advancing the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific. Measures endorsed or announced included the upgraded APEC Connectivity Blueprint for infrastructure and supply-chain work, a statement on harnessing digital technologies for jobs, an Asia-Pacific community studies center, a proposal to establish a World Association for Bay Areas Economic Cooperation, and financial support for practical cooperation.
items.title: Wang Yi frames APEC Shenzhen meeting as a new peak in Asia-Pacific cooperation

items.summary: Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is conducting a seven-day tour of Asia as part of a strategy to reduce Canada's dependence on the United States and build new economic partnerships in one of the world's fastest-growing regions. The framing that this represents an effort to 'redraw' Canada's relationship with the world comes from CGTN, which reported the trip; it is not independently confirmed here.
items.title: Mark Carney's Asian tour aims to diversify Canada's trading partners

items.summary: The BBC reports that up to 100,000 young EU people per year could be allowed to travel, work and study in the UK under a new youth mobility scheme expected to be agreed at the UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday, with an equal number of British youths permitted into Europe. The proposal traces to an 2024 EU offer allowing 18- to 30-year-olds to stay up to four years; Labour rejected it then as freedom of movement and now proposes a time-limited scheme capping numbers and barring benefit claims, though the UK's number cap remains a reported sticking point alongside demands that EU students pay domestic tuition fees. Downing Street has not commented on details but said talks were "down to the wire" Thursday, with Burnham citing lower food prices, reduced business costs, less red tape, and an immigration Channel action plan as benefits of any deal; his spokesman says legislation would follow next week if a deal is secured. Trade agreement could remove export checks for UK food firms while requiring adherence to EU rules on gene-edited crops and labelling, with the government estimating £5bn added to the economy from trade alone. The scheme fits broader debate over rejoining Europe: Burnham has ruled out major changes before the next election; Badenoch wants easier trading "not at any cost" and warned of EU rule compliance for non-trading firms; Farage called it a costly error without democratic mandate; Davey said Labour should go further, including returning to freedom of movement. All figures are reported claims attributed to their sources rather than established outcomes.
items.title: UK-EU youth mobility scheme reported as near-agreement ahead of summit

items.summary: A coronial inquest into four infant deaths in NSW's northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024 heard that each baby might have survived had standard antenatal scans, monitoring and follow-up been applied. Baby DH died about eight hours after a free birth attended by a doula but no medical professionals; neonatologist associate professor Nicholas Evans said his complex heart abnormalities would have been detectable on routine scan and referred to paediatric cardiology, while cardiologist Dr Paul Brooks called it 'highly likely' all abnormalities would have shown pre-birth. Baby D's mother did not know she was carrying twins until discovering a stillborn second twin; experts agreed the cause of death is unknown but most likely respiratory distress from compromised heart function, with root cause being that the twin pregnancy went undiagnosed before birth. Baby R died after a free birth at 43 weeks and one day; Evans identified as 'root cause' Kali's advice to date delivery from conception rather than an ultrasound putting birth in mid August instead of late July, breaching standard practice of ending pregnancies by 42 completed weeks. Baby B declined ultrasounds and a group B streptococcus test despite being warned repeatedly that hospital birth was needed for his twins; he likely died of GBS pneumonia and sepsis while antibiotics would have helped many infected babies in hospital. The women cited traumatic experiences, distrust of clinicians and lack of services as reasons for free or home births. The inquest is ongoing.
items.title: NSW coronial inquest: four babies who died after free or home births may have survived with routine checks

items.summary: The Lion Academy Trust, which runs Barclay primary school in Leyton, east London, has issued a formal apology and agreed substantial compensation for four British Muslim children aged six to 10 who were told they could be referred to the counter-extremism programme or local hate crime teams after wearing items displaying Palestinian colours at a November 2023 Children in Need fundraising day. The letters went to parents, prompting them to launch a legal challenge when no apology followed; the case was heard at Central London county court on Thursday. Lawyers for the children alleged direct and indirect discrimination plus harassment on grounds of race, ethnicity, religion and belief, together with breaches of freedom of expression and thought. Shahid Achhala, father of one child represented by Leigh Day and supported by Prevent Watch, said his eight-year-old son was subjected to mistreatment causing emotional distress; Layla Aitlhadj of Prevent Watch described the families as vindicated after three years of pressure. The trust has been approached for comment.
items.title: Lion Academy Trust to pay compensation after Prevent referral threat over children's Palestine badges

items.summary: Japanese government data released earlier this week show the economy shrank an annualized 0.1% in the July-September quarter, its first contraction in a year, as private consumption fell 0.3% from the previous quarter. Analysts note that explanations for the decline—citing a Kumamoto Prefecture earthquake, heavy rains, and reduced air conditioner demand—all point to temporary factors rather than structural weakness; however, some analysts argue the slump may be worse than it initially appears.
items.title: Japan's GDP contraction raises concerns it may be deeper than temporary factors suggest

items.summary: The leaders of China, the US and Russia met for 90 minutes on Nov 19 at an APEC side event in Shenzhen, issuing a joint declaration pledging talks on nuclear risks, energy supply cooperation and UN reform. Analysts say all three walked away claiming gains: Xi gained hosting prestige as a convening power; Trump projected global leadership and put nuclear arms control on the agenda; Russia's status was elevated with its top-level isolation from the US effectively ended, reinforced by declaration language protecting state officials' immunities amid Putin's ICC warrant. The declaration offered no timetable, mechanisms or plan for follow-up meetings. Analysts differ on whether closer coordination bolsters global stability or grants the three greater sway: Chong Ja Ian of NUS read Xi's references to core interests and red lines as implying a three-way division of the world, while Wu Xinbo of Fudan saw it instead as addressing shared challenges without dividing spheres of influence. On nuclear risks specifically, experts view talks rather than cuts as the realistic near-term outcome: Salisbury of IISS notes New START expired in February 2025 and that modernisation makes reductions unlikely on a long road; Wu suggested preventing AI control over nuclear weapons could be discussed. Stockholm International Peace Research Institute estimates China holds about 620 warheads versus roughly 5,042 for the US and 5,420 for Russia. Concrete action remains thin: Wang Dan of Eurasia Group called the energy pledge a possible positive spillover but noted it specified no quantities or timetable; Putin said leaders had not agreed to meet regularly in this format, though Wu believes further rounds could occur within two years.
items.title: Xi-Trump-Putin trilateral summit in Shenzhen produced a joint declaration with no binding commitments

items.summary: Honda unveiled the Avancier, a six-seat flagship hybrid SUV slated for sale next spring in Japan, China and Australia but not the U.S., where its sales fell 53% in September. Built mainly in Thailand with an undisclosed price, it will sit above the CR-V as the first model using Honda's new drivetrain pairing a more powerful engine with a more efficient electric motor. The launch is part of Honda's plan to introduce 15 new gas-electric models by March 2030 and its pivot away from fully electric cars after ill-timed EV investments triggered a ¥2.5 trillion ($15.7 billion) impairment charge and the company's first annual loss; it also plans a $3 billion Ohio factory for next-generation hybrids. Product planner Junichi Miyahara said Honda wants to strengthen its foothold in large vehicles, where its share trails competitors, while analyst Tatsuo Yoshida warned that abandoning EVs entirely could expose Honda as demand shifts again.
items.title: Honda launches hybrid Avancier SUV as it pivots from EVs

items.summary: City authorities reported that Russian missile and drone strikes on Kyiv on Friday killed three people and damaged two bridges, according to the mayor. The attack followed Vladimir Putin's vow of 'much more painful' retaliation after Ukraine this week struck the Crimea bridge connecting Russia-annexed Crimea to mainland Ukraine. A separate liveblog entry reports US envoy Jared Kushner told President Volodymyr Zelensky he believes Russia is comfortable with NATO-like security guarantees for postwar Ukraine, while a third entry describes a summit in Shenzhen attended by Xi Jinping, Putin and Donald Trump where Putin said the three nations share interests in settling regional conflicts including Ukraine's.
items.title: Russian attacks killed three and damaged two bridges in Kyiv

items.summary: Sean Cairncross, the US national cyber director who advises the president on cybersecurity policy and strategy while coordinating cyber efforts across federal agencies, was dismissed from his role following a series of technology outages affecting travel, communications, banking, and an internal National Security Agency system. A source close to the White House told AFP that Kirsten Davies, currently acting as principal advisor for information management, IT, cybersecurity, and information assurance to Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, will take over on a temporary basis; State Secretary Marco Rubio posted congratulations on social media. The office was first established in 2021, and the Trump administration released a seven-page cyber strategy document in March pledging to disable cyber threats through streamlined regulations, modernised federal systems, hardened infrastructure, and AI advantage.
items.title: US national cyber director Sean Cairncross fired after wave of tech outages

items.summary: The Chinese embassy in Japan warned its nationals on Tuesday to avoid climbing Mount Fuji during the closed season, citing strong winds and blizzards with no operational shelter or first-aid facilities. The warning follows the disappearance of Chen Jie, 25, who vanished on 8 November while attempting an ascent alone after his two companions turned back; his family is reportedly offering 500,000 yuan ($75,000) for information leading to his recovery and 100,000 yuan if his body is found. The embassy's concern is that the large reward could encourage ill-prepared climbers to attempt dangerous off-season ascents; Mount Fuji's official climbing season runs from around early July to early September. Separately, Yamanashi prefectural authorities announced earlier this year that rescues by helicopter for off-peak climbers will be self-funded and that detailed climbing plans will be required, with governor Kotaro Nagasaki stating these measures aim to change perceptions of winter climbing. On Wednesday, Nagasaki said search efforts could trigger "secondary disasters" and appeared to appeal directly to Chen's family via a Mainichi Shimbun report, urging them not to endanger others; some Japanese social media users have similarly expressed fears the reward may tempt reckless climbers. Yamanashi police reported that Chen pressed on alone from the fifth station of the Yoshida Trail at around 2,300m after his friends turned back, and a friend last heard from him via video message at 10:30; authorities launched a search on 10 November but had to halt it several times due to poor weather. The reward figure is reported by Chinese and Japanese media without confirmation of when Chen's father posted the offer.
items.title: Chinese embassy warns citizens against off-season Mount Fuji climbs amid missing climber's reward

items.summary: Nepal observes Kaag Tihar, a festival honoring house crows as divine messengers, but Kathmandu's human-crow relations face strain from habitat loss and unmanaged refuse. Satellite analysis attributes a 124% expansion to urban sprawl between 1989 and 2018, while another study found municipal green space fell by 54% between 1975 and 2025; the removal of more than 2,000 mature trees along major roads has pushed crows (Corvus splendens) to nest on utility poles. Bird ecologist Hem Bahadur Katuwal attributes this shift to habitat destruction leaving only adaptable generalist species like crows behind. Unmanaged refuse—open dumping and uncovered meat-shop waste—has drawn dense crow and black kite concentrations, with ornithologist Kamal Raj Gosai noting that exposed food accelerates their crowding while crows serve as scavengers feeding on carcasses. This aggregation fueled an H5N1 outbreak at Nepal's Central Zoo linked to wild crows moving across the city, causing loss or culling of more than 60 animals; veterinarian Krishna Prasad Acharya says crows occupy an unusual ecological niche spanning garbage dumps, poultry farms, and human settlements that escalates cross-species disease risk. Katuwal argues eliminating urban crows is misguided since they clean waste, placing the blame on poor waste management and habitat destruction rather than the birds themselves. Kathmandu acting mayor Sunita Dangol reports incorporating bird conservation into environmental policy by removing decorative tree lights, adjusting road plans to preserve mature trees, and developing planting guidelines with botanists.
items.title: Kathmandu's urban sprawl and waste are reshaping crow populations ahead of Kaag Tihar

items.summary: The Yorke and Northern Local Health Network (YNLHN) announced it would discontinue a one-team, one-site birthing model at the Jamestown and Crystal Brook hospitals, abandoning the trial about one month into its planned six-month run. The change followed local clinicians advising they would not participate; GPs had written to the health minister with "urgent concern" that the rostering restricted doctors from holding maternity and emergency on-call roles simultaneously while complicating handovers. YNLHN governing board chair John Voumard said the trial aimed to address workforce shortages and non-compliance with SA Health rostering requirements, which he said were met at only these two sites in the state; he insisted compliant rosters require five doctors per site per roster 365 days a year and that this requirement would not change. Both hospitals will continue birthing services only when they meet the rostering requirement. SASMOA chief industrial officer Bernadette Mulholland said practitioners did not agree with the network's "rostering position" and described it as "unsustainable." SA Health had paused birthing services for one month in June over a workforce shortage, and there were 41 diversions from Jamestown and Crystal Brook between July 2025 and June 2026. A petition against the trial attracted more than 10,000 signatures before closing; Member for Stuart Geoff Brock said he would table it in parliament next week seeking an inquiry into the YNLHN board amid community frustration over communication. Private midwife Chrissy Mackinnon described herself as "absolutely thrilled" by the reversal but agreed that lack of clear communication was a significant issue, while Voumard attributed wider community concerns to misinformation and said birthing families would face uncertainty under the previous system unless there were more local doctors and midwives.
items.title: SA Mid North birthing-model trial abandoned after community backlash

items.summary: Large demonstrations in the Czech Republic challenged Prime Minister Andrej Babiš's plans to change the funding model of public broadcasters. Mikuláš Minář, Chair of the Million Moments for Democracy movement, joined François Picard from Prague on Spotlight, warning that his country risks following Hungary and Slovakia into democratic backsliding by citing their leaders Orbán and Fico as models to avoid. Marking the anniversary of the 1989 Velvet Revolution, Minář recalled the freedoms gained after communism's fall and called for stronger opposition parties and continued public mobilisation. He clarified that his group is a civil movement rather than an electoral party.
items.title: Czechs protest against Babiš's public broadcaster funding changes amid democracy concerns

items.summary: Nearly 1,689 David Jones employees were served redundancy notices on Friday, with employment set to terminate December 30. The redundancies follow the retailer's entry into voluntary administration earlier in the month and its announced closure of 19 of its 38 stores across Australia and New Zealand on November 11. Union SDA NSW secretary Bernie Smith said it would seek alternative employment for members, noting companies had already come forward to offer roles; the union also established a help desk over entitlements. Retail analyst Gary Mortimer called the news 'deeply disappointing' and warned that losing around 1,500 positions would add pressure on Australia's labour market as its unemployment rate sits at 4.9 per cent. The ABC confirmed David Jones is up to date with superannuation for its 6,000 employees under new pay-day laws from July; the company said customers' entitlements will be paid but delivery options such as click and collect are unavailable while online orders surge amid longer expected deliveries.
items.title: David Jones redundancy notices issued to nearly 1,700 staff amid Christmas-period closure

items.summary: At the 2026 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) CEO Summit in Shenzhen, industry executives reported that global investors are shifting from treating Chinese assets as short-term trading opportunities toward holding them for asset allocation and long-term returns. He Yiwei, CEO of Zhong Ou Asset Management International Limited, attributed this to China's financial opening-up expanding its share of the global economy and said overseas long-term investors including sovereign wealth funds have steadily increased their investments; he also called for wider access to cross-border products and more consistent Asia-Pacific rules for digital connectivity and green finance. Ho Yiu-tung, co-CEO of JPMorgan China, characterized China's opening as moving beyond expanded market access toward closer alignment with international rules, noting the bank has operated in the country for 105 years; he cited that China has the world's second-largest stock and bond markets. Ernesto Torres Cantu, Citi's head of international, said APEC member economies' trade grew sharply over the past decade to about half of global trade, creating cross-border sourcing, sales, and investment opportunities. These are claims made by executives at a summit; none were independently verified in the text.
items.title: Executives say global investors increasingly treat Chinese assets as long-term holdings at 2026 APEC CEO Summit

items.summary: Sensor Tower estimates GTA 6 generated $2.36 billion in revenue from pre-orders and launch-day sales on its November 19 release, with 24.58 million copies sold by Thursday evening; these figures are the platform's own estimates rather than confirmed data. Rockstar Games and parent company Take-Two have not published official numbers, though demand has been described as "unprecedented." For comparison, Take-Two reported that GTA V generated more than $800 million in retail sales during its first 24 hours (excluding Japan and Brazil launches) and shipped nearly 235 million copies overall. The article's revenue figure is an estimate from a third-party analytics firm; the official figures remain unverified by the game's developer or publisher.
items.title: GTA 6 estimated launch revenue and sales per Sensor Tower, unconfirmed by Rockstar or Take-Two

items.summary: Sean Cairncross is leaving as White House national cyber director following a week of technology-related service disruptions affecting air travel, banking, communications and e-commerce, including the National Security Agency. Secretary of State Marco Rubio named Kirsten Davies to succeed him in an acting capacity; she was previously the Pentagon's Chief Information Officer. Officials say there is no evidence of a cyberattack, attributing the outages instead to technology failures. Cairncross had been nominated by Trump and confirmed by the Senate in 2025 for his role as top adviser on cybersecurity and data protection policy.
items.title: White House replaces national cyber director after tech outages

items.summary: At the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in Shenzhen, China, on November 20, 2026, leaders released two documents calling for greater regional connectivity and fewer trade barriers. The APEC Connectivity Blueprint emphasized strengthening land, maritime and air transport networks and called for digital transformation of transport systems, including exploring safe autonomous technologies; it reaffirmed the forum's commitment to the Putrajaya Vision 2040. In a separate statement titled the 2026 APEC Leaders' Shenzhen Outlook, leaders acknowledged complex global challenges alongside emerging opportunities and pledged to maintain macroeconomic stability while promoting productivity and economic growth. The documents describe these commitments as voluntary, nonbinding and consensus-based; they do not establish binding obligations or report specific infrastructure investments.
items.title: APEC leaders call for stronger regional connectivity at Shenzhen summit

items.summary: Heavy fighting occurred along a key route through Port-au-Prince as Haiti's National Police, with the UN-backed anti-gang task force and private firm Vectus Global, conducted an operation in Martissant on Thursday that killed at least 34 suspected gangsters. The police posted footage of armoured vehicles moving through the neighbourhood, which local media described as having heavy gunfire and explosive drones; the area has been overrun by gangs for five years since rival groups began fighting to control it in 2021. Police said operations are entering a new phase aimed at increasing pressure on gang networks, dismantling strongholds, and extending control over strategic areas including Tabarre in Port-au-Prince and the Artibonite region. El Salvador also deployed about 2,500 troops to Haiti last month after four of their own went missing following an attack on 18 October; under President Nayib Bukele's orders they recently attacked two gang leaders' homes but neither Jeff nor Lanmò San Jou was killed.
items.title: Haitian armed forces launch Martissant operation killing at least 34 suspected gang members

items.summary: The FIFA U-17 Men's World Cup opened on 19 November 2026 in Qatar. The article states this is the second time Qatar has hosted the tournament, after its first hosting in 2025, and claims it will host for five consecutive years through 2029—presented as a plan rather than an established fact. This edition features 48 teams and more than 104 matches across the full competition; on opening day alone, eight matches were played with Uganda and Egypt among those in action, and more than 10 African nations are competing to improve on previous results.
items.title: FIFA U-17 Men's World Cup opening day in Qatar, 2026

items.summary: According to Focus Taiwan, TSMC's subsidiary TSMC Partners bought 6,024,096 Anthropic shares for about USD 500 million at the company's IPO price of USD 83 each. The deal was disclosed in a Thursday filing and is structured as an equity investment paid in a lump sum under Rule 144 of the US Securities Act of 1933. It follows TSMC's November 10 board decision to authorise up to USD 500 million each for Anthropic common shares and OpenAI Group preferred shares, signalling interest in both AI developers; this transaction confirms only the Anthropic portion while a separate authorisation covers OpenAI. Anthropic debuted on Nasdaq on November 19 after raising about USD 81.34 billion at an IPO that valued it near USD 1.5 trillion from 980 million shares priced at USD 83; its shares opened at USD 111.50, a 34.34 per cent premium, then closed at USD 97.17, up 17.07 per cent, with market capitalisation around USD 1.44 trillion.
items.title: TSMC acquires a small Anthropic stake at IPO price via its subsidiary

items.summary: Shares of Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCL Tech and Tech Mahindra rose up to 4% on Friday as a sharp rout in AI-linked equities rattled sentiment. Nvidia fell over 3%, while AMD and Micron dropped up to 7%; Korean beneficiaries Samsung and SK Hynix each tumbled 7%. This occurred despite Anthropic's IPO listing at a 34% premium, which the article frames as failing to revive confidence in AI trades amid broader US selling that pushed equities toward session lows. Asian markets extended losses heading for their worst weekly performance since 2020: MSCI Asia-Pacific fell 2.5%, on track for a six-day losing streak and down 7% for the week; Japan's Nikkei dropped 4.1% (6.8% weekly loss) and South Korea's KOSPI fell 4.7% (set to finish 7.5% lower). The article attributes AI-stock pressure partly to Jensen Huang's departure from Nvidia, an anti-data-centre movement following Democrats' midterm gains, sector debt concerns, and extinction warnings about artificial intelligence. Global brokerage Jefferies named Coforge and Sagility as top picks, citing improved growth and net hiring but soft deal bookings and rising subcontractor usage that signal limited confidence in sustained expansion; it noted aggregate operating margins expanded 25 basis points sequentially to 19.9%, led by a 130-basis-point jump at HCLTech, 45 basis points at Wipro and 35 basis points at Tech Mahindra, with other IT companies' margins largely flat. Jefferies is bearish on TCS, HCL Tech, Wipro and Tech Mahindra, assigning an Underperform rating to each; these are brokerage views from a note by Veer Sharma, who the article states is not SEBI-registered and holds no financial interest in the named companies.
items.title: Indian IT stocks rally up to 4% amid global AI selloff despite Anthropic's premium IPO

items.summary: Anthropic began trading on Nasdaq Thursday with a market value of USD 1.75 trillion, becoming the largest public stock offering ever recorded and breaking that record five years before its debut. The company's founders split from OpenAI to prioritize AI safety while building Claude; CEO Dario Amodei called the push between safety and advancement one of "central tensions at the heart of the company." He likened rapid model self-improvement to raising a car's speed limit, saying Anthropic chose to drive at 90 miles per hour rather than 200 while spending surplus effort on safe development. Internal researcher Jacob Coxon resigned in September after warning both Anthropic and OpenAI are "gambling with our lives," prompting Amodei to call for an industry-wide slowdown; a Model Evaluation and Threat Research report found Anthropic developing systems at twice its prior-year pace, largely aided by AI itself. As a public benefit corporation legally required to balance shareholder interests with the public good, Anthropic's IPO concentrated extreme wealth among founders—each sibling's net worth rose from just over USD 14 billion before the offering to roughly USD 22.7-22.8 billion afterward—though they have pledged voluntary commitments of 80 percent equity to philanthropy and at least 5 percent of stock to a public benefit fund. The company devoted 93 pages in an SEC filing to risk factors including catastrophic or existential threats, drawing criticism that it frames dystopian outcomes while positioning itself as the solution; a September SNL sketch mocked this contradiction with Amodei saying "we do not condone what we are doing," echoed on a protest sign outside Anthropic's San Francisco headquarters reading "I urge you to urge me to stop."
items.title: Anthropic IPOs at $1.75 trillion valuation amid safety-advancement tensions

items.summary: A US court granted final approval in July 2026 to a settlement under which Anthropic agreed to pay $1.5 billion to settle a class-action lawsuit brought by authors who accused the company of downloading pirated books, including from Library Genesis and Pirate Library Mirror, to train its AI models; the agreement covers more than 480,000 works allegedly obtained from those pirate libraries. The settlement followed a distinction drawn by a federal judge in 2025 that using copyrighted books to train AI could qualify as fair use but making and retaining copies of pirated books was not protected. Anthropic's settlement did not establish that all AI training using copyrighted material is illegal.
items.title: Anthropic settles copyright class-action lawsuit for $1.5 billion

items.summary: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained at the NYT DealBook Summit that the company's voluntary exit offer for around 60,000 employees—more than a quarter of its workforce—is intended to give staff agency amid an AI rebuild rather than replace engineers with automation. He argued software engineering will thrive but in reorganized form, pointing to Cowork's team of just 11 developers who build "a software factory that builds the product." The buyout follows an open letter from current and former employees describing work as "joyless and demoralizing," citing AI targets, stagnant pay with some merit raises below 1%, and demands for treating AI as assistive rather than a labor replacement. Microsoft confirmed the Voluntary Exit Offer on October 26 covering vice president-level staff at VP level and below on select teams in the US, Canada, India and UK; employees have until December 9 to decide, with acceptors leaving December 31 after eight weeks' base pay, though fewer than 5% are expected to take it. Chief people officer Amy Coleman told the NYT the buyouts were not linked to AI's impact on work and did not rule out future layoffs. The offer comes alongside a strong quarter: profit of $36.6 billion up 32%, capital spending rising 30% to $45.2 billion, with roughly $170 billion expected this year. For those who stay, employees report that departing colleagues' work will fall on remaining staff rather than be replaced.
items.title: Nadella defends Microsoft's 60,000-employee buyout as AI-driven reorganization

items.summary: The International Energy Agency published its World Energy Outlook 2026 during the COP31 climate summit, warning that a prolonged disruption to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz could reduce oil flows through the waterway from 20 million barrels per day before the crisis to under 2 million by 2035 as countries invest in alternative supply routes. IEA executive director Fatih Birol said he sees no credible pathway for energy markets to return to their pre-crisis state, though he noted considerable resilience so far; his member and association countries account for 75% of global energy demand. The report projects that even under an extreme scenario of reduced oil use, the Middle East would remain the world's largest exporter of oil to international markets. Renewables led by solar photovoltaic and nuclear power are expected to be the biggest beneficiaries of a pivot toward domestic resources, with biofuels and energy efficiency also gaining ground; in Asia, coal could see extended reliance amid energy security concerns. India is cited as a leading example of reshaping its energy system around clean sources: it reached 50% non-fossil installed power capacity by 2025, five years ahead of schedule, with solar PV expected to drive most additional generation over the next decade and coal-fired output taking a smaller share than in the previous decade. India's annual energy investment is projected to grow 85% over the next decade at an average of $200 billion per year, while renewables and nuclear are expected to raise their combined electricity-generation share from 28% in 2025 to 51% by 2035 under the Stated Policies Scenario. Under a more ambitious Accelerated Roadmap Case, India could cut oil requirements by 580,000 barrels per day by 2035 versus STEPS through faster electric-vehicle adoption and electrification; its natural gas consumption would also fall 8% below STEPS. These figures are the IEA's projections under named scenarios rather than observed outcomes.
items.title: IEA warns of lasting Strait of Hormuz shock and hails India's clean energy shift in 2026 outlook

items.summary: The Free Press Journal's midday guide bundles ten unrelated developments without ranking them by significance. Cyclone Akvan began landfall near Gopalpur in Odisha at 8 am Saturday with winds of 70-90 kmph; about 3 lakh people were evacuated and 423 rescue teams deployed, per the report. The gangster Naseem Durrani was killed in a joint Delhi Police-Noida STF encounter in Bulandshahr, UP. Anthropic's IPO reportedly turned over 5,100 employees into millionaires with an $81 billion listing that lifted its market valuation to nearly $1.8 trillion; the figures are attributed as reports rather than confirmed results. In cricket, New Zealand were bowled out for 368 on Day 2 of their first Test against India at Henry Nicholls' unbeaten 175 and Glenn Phillips' 118, while Jasprit Bumrah took four wickets; India replied with 159/1 in 39 overs. Other items include an FPJ exclusive alleging a Chennai syndicate paid Rs 50,000 toward medical bills to lure an ice-cream seller into drug trafficking; SpiceJet receiving a seven-day DGCA show-cause notice over eight alleged violations including flight cancellations and delayed payments; Salesforce laying off a manager after 12 years; Google launching the Gemini 4 Neon model with four thinking levels, a one-million-token context window, and claims it completes tasks three times faster than Carbon at roughly 60% of the cost; and Kareena Kapoor attending K3G's 25th anniversary event. Most figures are reported or claimed by sources rather than independently verified.
items.title: FPJ noon news digest lists cyclone, Anthropic IPO, cricket and assorted headlines

items.summary: Google released Gemini 4 Neon as an intermediate option between Carbon (positioned for hard, long-horizon work) and Hydrogen (fast everyday execution), making it the fourth Gemini 4 model in roughly seven weeks. It offers four thinking levels up to extra-high with a one-million-token context window; Google claims tasks complete about three times faster than Carbon at around 60% of its cost, or 32% lower per-task cost at default high settings. On benchmarks, Neon ranks third on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (score 61) and second on the Vals Index, though Artificial Analysis describes the gain over Carbon as small—about 17% lower cost per task—and first on the Coding Agent Index (58.6). A cybersecurity version is set to roll out through Google's Fairwind Program, and safety claims include Carbon-level protections plus a 99.2% pass rate on an internal agent honesty evaluation. Pricing via API is $3 per million input tokens and $15 per million output tokens ($0.15 for cached input), higher than the current promotional rates of $2 and $10 for Carbon; Google's cost-per-task claims rest on Neon finishing work with fewer tokens rather than a lower per-token price. It is available through the Gemini API, AI Studio, business plans, paid Pro/Ultra app subscribers, and Antigravity.
items.title: Google launches Gemini 4 Neon, a mid-tier model in its Gemini 4 family

items.summary: The Nifty Metal index fell more than 6% across seven sessions to a low of 11,980 on Friday, with metal stocks including Tata Steel and Vedanta dropping up to 7% over five days. Copper slid nearly 4-5%, aluminium reached 2026 lows, and gold hit a 14-month low near $3,730-3,760. Vinit Bolinjkar of Ventura attributed the weakness to a stronger US dollar at roughly a 19-month high and hawkish Fed commentary, noting that higher real yields raise the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding commodities while tempering global demand expectations; these are his explanations rather than established facts about causation. Markets were pricing around a 90% probability of a 25 basis point hike at the December FOMC, with Waller's suggestion of a larger move adding to uncertainty. An analyst warned that sustained price weakness could pressure EBITDA margins and earnings even if volumes hold, though domestic steel demand may provide partial cushion; this is an opinion rather than a forecast outcome. Investors are watching the December FOMC result, LME copper and aluminium prices, and Chinese demand signals for signs of stabilisation.
items.title: Indian metals stocks fall sharply as prices hit multi-month lows on hawkish Fed expectations

items.summary: Nepal Prime Minister Balendra Shah will make a two-day State visit to India from November 22 to 23 at the invitation of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. A 34-member government delegation led by Shah is scheduled to travel from Kathmandu to New Delhi, where he holds planned talks with Modi on Monday, November 23. The itinerary includes joint inauguration of energy projects and signing or exchanging bilateral agreements covering various areas of cooperation. During the visit, Shah will address a joint press conference with Modi, receive a luncheon in his honour, call on President Droupadi Murmu, pay tribute to Mahatma Gandhi at Rajghat, and attend the Nepal-India Business Forum. A separate business delegation is also expected to accompany him. The invitation followed the formation of Shah's Rastriya Swatantra Party-led government in March, which came to power around six months after Gen Z protests toppled former PM K P Sharma Oli in September last year. Discussions are expected to cover rail, road and air connectivity, infrastructure development, cooperation, trade and tourism. The visit aligns with the longstanding convention under which newly elected Nepali prime ministers make India their first official bilateral destination, though this is not absolute since former PM Oli chose China for his 2024 first visit. Ahead of the trip, Indian Ambassador to Nepal Sudhakar Dalela met Shah on Wednesday to convey Modi's greetings and brief him on preparations; Shah thanked Modi and the Government of India for assistance after floods in the Rasuwa-Bhotekoshi region and congratulated Dalela on his appointment. The two countries share a 1,751-km open border with extensive people-topeople connections.
items.title: Nepal PM Shah's first State visit to India, November 22-23

items.summary: A Supreme Court bench headed by Chief Justice Surya Kant, with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, declined Friday to separately list a recall application seeking review of the September 23 split verdict on whether challenges to the 2023 law governing appointment of the Chief Election Commissioner and Election Commissioners should be heard by a larger bench. The court said both the recall plea and any challenge to the order referring the matter to a five-judge Constitution bench could instead be considered by that already constituted bench, which would decide the validity of the law; the CJI added this bench could hear the application even after one judge who delivered the split verdict retires. Advocate Prashant Bhushan argued for listing before the original two-judge bench (Justices Dipankar Datta and Satish Chandra Sharma), noting Justice Sharma was due to retire next week, alleging a conflict of interest on his part; he also contended that because the referral order itself had been challenged on alleged-conflict grounds, it should be heard by the same original bench. The CJI responded that Bhushan could raise these issues before the Constitution bench. At issue is the 2023 law's exclusion of the CJI from the panel selecting the ECs; under it, selection rests with the Prime Minister, the Lok Sabha opposition leader, and a Union cabinet minister. Justice Datta held challenges could be heard by a two-judge bench while Justice Sharma favored referral to a five-judge Constitution bench on account of important constitutional questions.
items.title: Supreme Court declines separate listing of plea challenging split verdict on EC law

items.summary: The gap between India's benchmark 10-year government bond yields and the Nifty 50's forward earnings yield has widened to about 1.95 percentage points, approaching the roughly 2-percentage-point threshold that has proven difficult to sustain historically; data compiled by Bloomberg shows the gap at around 7.27% versus a 5.3% forward earnings yield for the Nifty 50's 12-month forward earnings, up from about 1.24 percentage points at end-September when it was narrowest in 19 months. A widening gap signals that sovereign debt offers greater returns at lower risk than equities, dimming stock-market appeal and raising the discount rate applied to future corporate earnings; CLSA's Vikash Kumar Jain said limited room for further P/E rerating exists until earnings catch up, while Goldman Sachs' Sunil Koul factored in a 2-3% moderation of forward P/E over 12 months. Despite this pressure, several Wall Street firms remain bullish on India as a relative haven amid swings in tech-heavy Asian markets tied to the global AI trade: Goldman expects the Nifty at 28,500 by end-2027 (about 12% upside from Thursday's close) and Citigroup at 28,000, both expecting earnings growth rather than rising valuations to drive gains. Koul noted large bank weightings could provide insulation as lenders benefit from higher rates, but Jain said the easy part of the catch-up trade is done and stocks need more catalysts; further equity gains would hinge on stronger earnings or lower yields.
items.title: India's equity-bond earnings-yield gap nears a historically hard-to-sustain level

items.summary: The COP31 presidency in Antalya, Türkiye, released a second and final cover decision draft on November 19 calling for electricity's share of total final energy use to reach 35% globally by 2035. The wording is softer than the first draft: rather than a firm standalone mandate asking countries to contribute 'in a nationally determined manner,' the target became one of several concrete solutions under global cooperation, qualified by national circumstances and accompanied only by a general mention of support. Negotiating blocs rejected the earlier text; the Like-Minded Developing Countries bloc (around two dozen states including India, China and Bangladesh) said it would not back any recognition of the pledge, while the Arab Group and Russia also objected over fossil-fuel language. Further revisions were still being negotiated ahead of the summit's scheduled close on November 20. As of November 18, 75 countries and 94 institutions endorsed the goal, including Germany, the UK, Japan, South Korea, Canada and the EU. Supporters argue electrification is an efficiency gain: the IEA says electric vehicles are two to four times more efficient than petrol or diesel cars, RMI reports that of 606 exajoules entering the global system in 2019 only 227 did useful work (37% overall), and fossil inefficiency wastes over $4.6 trillion a year; the IEA also estimated fuel-importing countries could cut import bills by more than $400 billion annually by 2035. Climate Action Tracker says electricity met about 17% of final energy use in 2000, reached 24% in 2023 and would reach about 28% under current policies by 2035; reaching 35% requires an average annual increase almost four times the historical pace since 2000. The IEA estimates cost-effective electrification could raise the global rate to 33%. India, which has not backed the goal, drives domestic electrification partly to cut fuel imports and pollution: its fuel import bill was around ₹17.5 trillion in 2025 under a business-as-usual scenario that would lift electricity's share from 29% to 33% by 2045 while imports rise to ₹23.3 trillion, though overall generation rose from 1,168 billion units in 2015-16 to 1,824 BU in 2024-25; India faces a cumulative financing gap of $6.5 trillion by 2070 led by the power sector and needs about $8.05 trillion for its transition through 2050 against roughly $5.56 trillion available, with nearly $2.5 trillion to come from international climate finance.
items.title: COP31 draft softens global electrification target amid developing-country resistance

items.summary: The Bombay Stock Exchange issued an observation letter clearing a proposed restructuring in which SEIL would transfer its education business to Shanti Learning Initiatives via slump sale, after which Shanti Educational Initiatives is set to merge into GREW Energy, planned for stock exchange listing. Vinay Thadani, CEO and Director at GREW Energy, stated that the BSE observation letter was an important step in the group restructuring and on the path to listing. The board-approved share exchange ratio fixes 100 fully paid-up equity shares of GREW Energy for every 212 shares of Shanti Educational Initiatives, both with a face value of Rs 1.
